doc.title: Marty Grosz interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 4, 1995

title: Finding obscure tunes and why songs need vocals
summary: He gets tapes from friends and collections, laments that festival bands rarely play together, and says many songs need a vocal to mean something.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: That’s a pretty good analogy. Let me just, before we wrap up, ask, where do you find these tunes?

I get guys to send me tapes. And I buy those things downstairs. Like downstairs they have those collections — Ethel Waters, Bob Howard, Teddy Wilson—I’m just trying to think. You know those, I’ve heard all, not all, but a lot of the greats, the things you hear over and over again. You know the great ones. And then you go looking for oddball stuff to play. And guys make up tapes of oddball things. Cassettes of strange things. I have friends who send me stuff. Wonderful. Tunes I never heard in my life by groups I never heard. You know and I mix it up. And you get ideas from that. Yeah. It’s interesting. There’s a world, a wealth of material out there. It hasn’t been plumbed. And the guys at these — that’s the problem of course, we don’t play together ever enough. You used to play in a joint, you’d play five or six nights a week with the same guys. Man, you could play three months, four months with the same guys, and then come to one of these festivals. You’d steamroller ‘em. I mean everybody comes to these festivals, they’re always saying, “Um, what do you want to play, um.” “Well I don’t know that one too well, do you know this one?” “Well, how does the bridge go, oh, yeah.” And finally they always wind up playing “Undecided” or a riff on “I Got Rhythm” or you know, often the same kind of thing, and it would really be nice to have some group and do some of these things. That’s where the vocals come in. Most of those songs, a lot of those songs don’t mean a hell of a lot without vocals. To John Q. Public out there it’s a tune. But what does it mean? And if you can have somebody to sing it, then it gets a meaning. A nice tune for

example that Ivy Anderson sang with Ellington and Wingy Manone sang it on records, is “Isn’t Love the Strangest Thing.” You know, pretty melody, everything like that, but I dare say it wouldn’t mean much if you didn’t have a vocal to sing with it. And they say, “Oh gee, what a nice thought,” you know, “how romantic.”
